OK, I'll make an attempt at why this works. Someone please correct if I'm wrong:

I believe the ash contains potassium (K), which is left behind along with other noncombustible trace components of wood. Mixed with water, the K ionizes to K+ and generated OH- ions from water. The OH- reduces pH (by definition) and you get a basic solution of potassium hydroxide and whatever other crap was in the ash.

Fat is made of a glycerol with fatty acid chains attached to it. A base attacks the linkage and generates fatty acids with a polar head, which is a kind of molecule also called "soap". The glycerol just becomes an excess by product.

Because generally polar substances can mix with polar and nonpolar with nonpolar, the long nonpolar tails of these soap molecules get embedded in fats and grease on your dirty object, but the polar head can interact with water (which is also polar) and and thus the whole ball of grease, thanks to its cover of soap (imagine grease droplet:soap molecule:nonpolar tail:polar head::pincushion:pin:needle part:needle head) becomes "soluble" and can be washed away with water. When you put ash water on dirty things, the saponification reaction happens at lower efficiency (because of suboptimal concentrations, impurities and no heat to catalyze) but just enough to solubilized the grease.

This is also how you make soap. Filter and sediment the ash water to remove most of the insoluble impurities and get cleaner KOH solution (aka lye). Dry to get pure KOH (caustic, strong base, watch out!). Then mix water, an oil (animal or vegetable) and the KOH in proportion as per the reaction and heat. Then filter out the water overnight and dry. Or with some vegetable fats you can end up with a liquid soap.

If you put KOH pellets on your hands by the way, it feels very slick, and this is why. The KOH saponifies the natural fatty coat of your skin using the skin's own moisture, and the resting soap feels slippery. Don't do this though, it's bad for your skin.
